subject: biology
topicDisplay: D3–D4 — Continuity and change: organisms and ecosystems
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
Why sperm are small and many, eggs large and few
What happens at fertilization in humans
Self-incompatibility keeps gametes from different plants
How a plant cross is done
Thermoregulation: sensors, control centre, hormone, effectors
What humans have added to the atmosphere

questions.q: What is the relative advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
options: Its offspring carry new gene combinations, giving the variation needed for a changed environment.
Its offspring gain the particular features that a changed environment comes to require.
Its offspring are better adapted than the parent in every environment, so more of them survive.
Its offspring carry new alleles produced by meiosis, which asexual offspring cannot receive.
optionWhy: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.
A student who thinks variation is produced to meet a need picks this. Meiosis and fertilization generate new combinations blindly; the environment selects among them afterwards.
A student who believes sexual reproduction is always superior picks this. In a stable environment a well-adapted parent does better to copy its genotype asexually than to break it up.
A student who thinks meiosis makes new alleles picks this. New alleles arise only by mutation, in asexual lineages too; meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of existing alleles.
questions.explain: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with new combinations of alleles, so among them some are likely to be adapted to an environment that has changed. This is its relative advantage; asexual reproduction's is the faithful copying of a genotype already adapted to the existing environment.

questions.q: In a fish species the female lays a few hundred large eggs in a nest and the male releases many millions of tiny sperm over them. Which statement explains the difference in size and number?
options: Sperm must travel to the eggs, so they are small with few food reserves and can be produced cheaply in vast numbers.
Eggs are larger because each one carries far more of the genetic material than a sperm does.
The numbers should be equal since one sperm fertilizes one egg; the surplus sperm are defective ones.
Sperm are small because so many are made that only a little cytoplasm is available for each one.
optionWhy: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.
A student who equates cell size with DNA content picks this. Sperm and egg each contribute one haploid set; the egg's extra bulk is cytoplasm with food reserves.
A student who reasons back from one-to-one fertilization picks this. Vast numbers of normal sperm are released because only a tiny fraction complete the journey to an egg.
A student who reverses the cause picks this. Sperm are small because they must travel; being small and cheap is what makes it possible to produce so many.
questions.explain: The prime difference between the sexes is that the male gamete travels to the female gamete, so it is smaller with less food reserves than the egg. From this follow the differences in numbers of gametes.

questions.q: Which event occurs during fertilization in humans?
options: The whole sperm enters the egg, so the embryo inherits its mitochondria from both parents.
The sperm and egg nuclei fuse into a single diploid nucleus before any cell division occurs.
The sperm nucleus enters the egg but the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
Enzymes from the sperm digest a hole in the egg membrane to let the nucleus in.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the sperm entering as a complete cell picks this. Only the nucleus enters; the tail and mitochondria are destroyed.
A student who learned 'the nuclei fuse' at GCSE picks this. The nuclear membranes dissolve and the chromosomes join a mitosis that directly produces two diploid nuclei.
After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.
A student who extends the acrosome enzymes to the egg membrane picks this. Entry is by fusion of the two cell membranes; enzymes act only on the coat outside the membrane.
questions.explain: After the sperm's cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane, the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the tail and mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote.

questions.q: Where are the gametes of a flowering plant produced?
options: The pollen grains themselves are the male gametes and the ovules are the female gametes.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes inside ovules.
Male gametes are produced in the stigma and female gametes in the anther.
Male gametes are produced inside pollen grains and female gametes in the seeds.
optionWhy: A student who casts pollen as the plant's sperm picks this. Pollen grains and ovules are structures inside which the gametes are produced.
Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.
A student who has swapped the two central structures picks this. The anther produces pollen (male); the stigma receives it and belongs to the female carpel.
A student who backdates seeds to the flower picks this. The ovary contains ovules; an ovule becomes a seed only after its gamete has been fertilized.
questions.explain: Gametes are produced inside ovules (female, within the ovary) and inside pollen grains (male, within the anther); pollination and pollen tube growth bring them together.

questions.q: In a self-incompatible plant species, pollen from a flower lands on the stigma of the same flower and germinates, but no seed is set. Which statement about self-incompatibility explains this?
options: It works by physically preventing the flower's own pollen from ever landing on its stigma.
It prevents inbreeding, which would otherwise cause harmful new mutations in the offspring.
It stops a plant's own pollen from fertilizing its eggs, so preventing inbreeding.
It is needed because self-fertilization would be asexual and so produce clones.
optionWhy: A student who models it on separate flowers and timing picks this. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism: matching alleles in pollen and carpel are recognized and the pollen tube is stopped.
A student who explains genetic defects by mutation picks this. Inbreeding makes harmful recessive alleles already present more likely to be homozygous; it creates no alleles.
Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.
A student who thinks one parent means asexual picks this. Self-fertilization is still sexual reproduction; the problem is inbreeding, not cloning.
questions.explain: Self-pollination leads to inbreeding, which decreases genetic diversity and vigour. Genetic self-incompatibility mechanisms ensure the gametes fusing at fertilization are from different plants.

questions.q: A breeder wants to cross a tall pea plant with a dwarf pea plant to obtain an F1 generation. Which procedure is required, and why?
options: Place pollen from one plant on the stigma of the other, where it fuses with the female gamete, so there is no need to remove the anthers first
Remove the anthers from flowers of one plant, then transfer pollen from the other plant to their stigmas, because a pea flower would otherwise self-pollinate
Grow the two plants next to each other, because a pea flower cannot be fertilized by its own pollen and so has to be cross-pollinated by insects
Allow the tall plant to self-pollinate and cross its seedlings with the dwarf plant, because the F1 is produced from a parent's own offspring
optionWhy: A student who thinks the pollen grain is the gamete and that fertilization happens on the stigma picks this. The female gametes are in the ovary, and unless the anthers are removed the flower's own pollen may fertilize them, spoiling the cross.

Peas produce male and female gametes on the same plant and normally self-pollinate. To make a cross the breeder must prevent selfing by removing the anthers and then carry out pollination by hand, transferring pollen (which contains the male gametes) to the stigma so that a pollen tube can reach the female gametes in the ovary.

A student who assumes an organism cannot fertilize itself picks this. Peas readily self-pollinate and self-fertilize, which is exactly why the breeder has to intervene to obtain a cross between two different plants.

A student who has confused the generation labels picks this. The F1 generation is the direct offspring of the P generation cross between the tall and dwarf plants; no intermediate selfing is involved.
questions.explain: Peas produce male and female gametes on the same plant and normally self-pollinate. To make a cross the breeder must prevent selfing by removing the anthers and then carry out pollination by hand, transferring pollen (which contains the male gametes) to the stigma so that a pollen tube can reach the female gametes in the ovary.

questions.q: Which list gives a human trait due to genotype only, then a trait due to environment only, then a trait due to interaction between genotype and environment, in that order?
options: Adult height; a facial scar; skin colour
ABO blood group; adult height; a facial scar
ABO blood group; skin colour; adult height
ABO blood group; a scar; adult height
optionWhy: A student who thinks inherited traits are fixed by the genes alone files height as genotype only. Height is strongly influenced by nutrition and health during growth, so it is an interaction trait, not a genotype-only one.

A student who treats any observable trait as part of the heritable phenotype puts the scar with the traits that involve genotype. A scar is due to the environment only, and height, listed here as environment only, has a clear genetic component.

A student who credits sunlight with all variation in skin colour puts it as environment only. Skin colour depends on several genes as well as on exposure to sunlight, so it is an interaction trait, like height.

ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.
questions.explain: ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.

questions.q: PKU usually appears in a child whose parents are both unaffected. Which statement correctly describes phenylketonuria (PKU)?
options: It is caused by a dominant allele of an autosomal gene, which is why the condition is expressed in every person who carries it
It is caused by a recessive allele that prevents the body making phenylalanine, so affected people need extra phenylalanine in their diet
It is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene coding for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
It is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome, so it is expressed in males far more often than in females
optionWhy: A student who reasons that a condition that is expressed must be dominant picks this. PKU appears only in people homozygous for the mutant allele; heterozygous carriers are unaffected, which is the signature of a recessive allele.

A student who takes the name to mean a shortage of phenylalanine picks this. The missing enzyme converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates and the treatment is a diet low in phenylalanine, not rich in it.

PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.

A student who assumes that any recessive disorder appearing in the children of unaffected parents is sex-linked picks this. The PKU gene is autosomal, so the condition is equally frequent in males and females.
questions.explain: PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.

questions.q: Why is haemophilia far more common in males than in females?
options: The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, so that a father passes the condition directly to each one of his sons
Females who inherit the allele can only ever be carriers, because the female body cannot develop the condition
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele produces the condition, whereas a female needs two
The Y chromosome carries a second copy of the gene that is more often mutated than the copy on the X
optionWhy: A student who expects a male-biased condition to pass from father to son picks this. The gene is on the X chromosome; a father gives his Y to sons, so sons inherit the haemophilia allele only from their mother.

A student who believes females cannot have haemophilia picks this. A female with two Xh alleles does have haemophilia; the condition is rare in females because inheriting Xh from both parents is much less likely.

The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.

A student who thinks the X and Y carry the same genes picks this. The Y chromosome carries far fewer genes than the X and has no copy of the haemophilia gene, which is precisely why males have only one copy.
questions.explain: The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.

questions.q: For a class's heights, the first quartile is 150 cm, the median is 158 cm, the third quartile is 166 cm, and the minimum and maximum are 130 cm and 192 cm. Above what height would a data point be categorized as an outlier on a box-and-whisker plot?
options: 190 cm
182 cm
174 cm
259 cm
optionWhy: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.
A student who measures 1.5 × IQR from the median rather than from the third quartile gets 158 + 24 = 182 cm. The rule uses the quartiles: the upper limit is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
A student who adds 1.5 × IQR to the first quartile instead of the third gets 150 + 24 = 174 cm. The upper limit is measured from the third quartile, and the lower limit from the first.

A student who takes the range (192 − 130 = 62 cm) as the interquartile range gets 1.5 × 62 = 93 and 166 + 93 = 259 cm. The IQR is the length of the box, Q3 − Q1 = 16 cm, not the full range of the data.
questions.explain: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.

questions.q: Why are homeostatic variables controlled by negative feedback rather than by positive feedback?
options: Negative feedback responds to harmful changes, while positive feedback responds to beneficial ones.
Negative feedback lowers a variable that has risen, which is the usual direction of deviation.
Negative feedback opposes a change, returning the variable towards its set point.
Negative feedback keeps the variable fixed at the set point with no fluctuation.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'positive' and 'negative' as value judgements picks this. The words describe the direction of the response relative to the change, not whether the change is good or bad for the organism.
A student who equates 'negative' with 'decrease' picks this. Negative feedback also raises a variable that has fallen; it is defined by opposing the change, not by lowering.

In negative feedback the response reverses the deviation that triggered it, so the variable is pushed back towards the set point from either side. Positive feedback amplifies a change and would drive the variable ever further away, so it cannot maintain a set point.

A student who thinks homeostasis means perfect constancy picks this. Negative feedback produces small oscillations around the set point, because a response is only triggered after a deviation has occurred.
questions.explain: In negative feedback the response reverses the deviation that triggered it, so the variable is pushed back towards the set point from either side. Positive feedback amplifies a change and would drive the variable ever further away, so it cannot maintain a set point.

questions.q: What is the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation?
options: It passes on the core temperature measured by thermoreceptors in the skin to the effectors.
It generates heat itself whenever the blood flowing through it becomes too cold.
It monitors blood temperature and coordinates the responses of the effectors.
It secretes thyroxin directly into the blood to raise the metabolic rate.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the skin receptors measure the core picks this. Peripheral thermoreceptors detect skin and external temperature; the core temperature is measured by the hypothalamus itself from the blood.
A student who reads 'controls temperature' as 'does the warming' picks this. The hypothalamus is a control centre; heat is generated by effectors such as skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue.

The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.
A student who has attached thyroxin to the wrong gland picks this. Thyroxin is secreted by the thyroid gland; the hypothalamus acts on the pituitary gland, which stimulates the thyroid.
questions.explain: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the roles of mutation and sexual reproduction in generating the variation on which natural selection acts?
options: Sexual reproduction produces new alleles by combining together the DNA of two different parents
Mutation produces precisely the particular alleles that the environment requires for survival
Mutation produces new alleles, and sexual reproduction produces new combinations of alleles
A trait can spread only once a new mutation for it arises, as populations lack variation
optionWhy: A student who thinks mixing parental DNA makes new alleles picks this. Every allele in an offspring came from a parent; sexual reproduction creates new combinations, not new alleles.
A student who thinks mutations are directed by need picks this. Mutations are random changes in base sequence and occur whether or not they are useful; selection acts afterwards.

Mutation is the only source of new alleles. Meiosis and random fertilization then shuffle the alleles that already exist into new combinations in the offspring, so both processes contribute variation but in different ways.

A student who underestimates how much heritable variation an ordinary population already contains picks this. Mutation has been generating alleles continuously, so populations already carry the variation on which selection acts.
questions.explain: Mutation is the only source of new alleles. Meiosis and random fertilization then shuffle the alleles that already exist into new combinations in the offspring, so both processes contribute variation but in different ways.

questions.q: An unusually cold winter kills 70% of a population of lizards. The proportion killed is similar in crowded and in sparse populations. Which statement is correct?
options: Low temperature is a density-independent abiotic selection pressure: lizards better able to tolerate cold are likelier to survive and breed
Temperature cannot be a selection pressure, because the deaths were not the result of competition between the lizards
The cold acted as a density-dependent factor, because it killed such a large number of lizards in the population
The surviving lizards became more cold-tolerant during the winter and will pass this tolerance on to their offspring
optionWhy: Extreme temperature is an abiotic factor whose effect does not depend on population density. Provided cold tolerance is partly heritable, the survivors are not a random sample, so allele frequencies in the population change.
A student who equates selection with contests between organisms picks this. Any factor, biotic or abiotic, that affects survival according to heritable traits is a selection pressure.

A student who reads 'density-dependent' as 'kills a lot' picks this. Density dependence is about whether the proportion affected changes with crowding; here it did not, so the factor is density-independent.

A student who thinks individuals adapt and pass the change on picks this. Tolerance acquired during life is not encoded in the base sequence of genes; the survivors were those that already carried alleles for greater cold tolerance.
questions.explain: Extreme temperature is an abiotic factor whose effect does not depend on population density. Provided cold tolerance is partly heritable, the survivors are not a random sample, so allele frequencies in the population change.

questions.q: Male birds of paradise have elaborate, brightly coloured plumage and perform complex courtship displays, while females are dull. The plumage is costly to grow and makes males easier for predators to see. Which explains how this plumage evolved?
options: Females mate preferentially with males whose plumage signals overall fitness, so alleles for elaborate plumage rise in frequency
The plumage cannot have evolved by selection, because a trait that lowers survival is selected against rather than favoured
The plumage evolved by artificial selection, because each female deliberately chooses which male's traits are passed on
Males that display more often grow brighter plumage during their lives and pass the brighter plumage on to their sons
optionWhy: This is sexual selection. Differences in physical and behavioural traits that act as signs of overall fitness affect success in attracting a mate, so males with the most elaborate plumage leave more offspring despite the survival cost.
A student who thinks selection is only about survival picks this. Fitness includes reproduction; if the gain in mating success outweighs the survival cost, the alleles for the plumage spread.

A student who equates 'choice' with artificial selection picks this. Artificial selection is deliberate choice of traits by humans; mate choice within a species is a selection pressure arising in the animal's own environment, with no human involved.
A student who thinks acquired characteristics are inherited picks this. Plumage developed through use is not encoded in genes; the alleles for elaborate plumage were inherited and selected.
questions.explain: This is sexual selection. Differences in physical and behavioural traits that act as signs of overall fitness affect success in attracting a mate, so males with the most elaborate plumage leave more offspring despite the survival cost.

questions.q: Why is a sealed glass vessel preferable to an open tank for a mesocosm used to investigate ecosystem stability?
options: It forms a completely closed system, so neither matter nor energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
The lid can be removed briefly each day to replace the oxygen that the organisms inside have used up.
It reproduces the natural ecosystem exactly, so any result obtained can be applied directly to the real ecosystem.
Matter cannot enter or leave the vessel, but light can still enter and heat can still leave.
optionWhy: A student who thinks sealing shuts out energy as well as matter picks this. Glass transmits light, so energy enters continuously; only matter is prevented from entering or leaving.

A student who thinks oxygen must be supplied from outside picks this. In a balanced mesocosm oxygen released by photosynthesis is recycled through respiration, and opening the vessel would defeat the purpose of sealing it.

A student who thinks a model is an exact copy picks this. A mesocosm is a simplified model; sealing it does not make it identical to a natural ecosystem, and its results must be interpreted with caution.

Sealing makes the mesocosm closed to matter, so nutrients must be recycled within it as in a stable ecosystem, while the glass allows energy transfer: light enters to drive photosynthesis and heat leaves.
questions.explain: Sealing makes the mesocosm closed to matter, so nutrients must be recycled within it as in a stable ecosystem, while the glass allows energy transfer: light enters to drive photosynthesis and heat leaves.

questions.q: Which practice increases the sustainability of agriculture on a farm?
options: Applying extra inorganic fertilizer every year so that all the nutrients lost by leaching are replaced.
Growing cover crops between harvests so that the soil is protected from erosion and less nitrate is leached away.
Ploughing sloping fields deeply each year, because soil is replaced by weathering as fast as it is lost.
Replacing manure with manufactured nitrogen fertilizer, since the fertilizer adds nothing to the farm's carbon footprint.
optionWhy: A student who thinks more fertilizer means more sustainability picks this. Fertilizer beyond what the crop takes up is itself leached, pollutes water and carries a large carbon footprint from its manufacture.

Soil erosion and leaching of nutrients are two of the factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture. Plant cover holds the soil, takes up nitrate that would otherwise leach, and reduces the need for fertilizer inputs.
A student who thinks soil regenerates quickly picks this. Soil forms over centuries, and bare ploughed slopes lose it rapidly to erosion, which permanently reduces the land's capacity to grow crops.

A student who thinks carbon footprint means only fuel burned on the farm picks this. Manufacturing nitrogen fertilizer uses large amounts of energy from natural gas, so it adds substantially to the carbon footprint.
questions.explain: Soil erosion and leaching of nutrients are two of the factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture. Plant cover holds the soil, takes up nitrate that would otherwise leach, and reduces the need for fertilizer inputs.

questions.q: Why does mercury released from industry reach high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna?
options: Large fish swallow the greatest volume of water while feeding, so they take in more mercury than smaller fish do.
Mercury taken in with prey is retained in tissues rather than excreted, so its concentration rises at each trophic level up to the tuna.
Tuna swim through polluted water for years and absorb mercury through their gills rather than from their food.
Tuna live for many years, so they accumulate mercury over time; smaller fish would reach the same level if they lived as long.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the top consumer simply takes in more picks this. The concentration in tuna comes from mercury already concentrated in the prey fish it eats, not from the water it swallows.

This is biomagnification. Mercury in water and sediments is converted by bacteria to methylmercury, which is taken up by small organisms, retained rather than excreted and passed on at increasing concentration along the food chain, so long-lived top predators such as tuna carry the highest concentrations.
A student who thinks uptake is direct from the environment picks this. Uptake across the gills is minor; the high concentration comes from eating prey that already contain methylmercury.

A student who equates biomagnification with lifetime accumulation picks this. Age contributes, but a tuna's food is itself already more concentrated than the water, and each trophic level adds a further step.
questions.explain: This is biomagnification. Mercury in water and sediments is converted by bacteria to methylmercury, which is taken up by small organisms, retained rather than excreted and passed on at increasing concentration along the food chain, so long-lived top predators such as tuna carry the highest concentrations.

questions.q: Which is an anthropogenic cause of the rise in the atmospheric concentration of methane since pre-industrial times?
options: Exhalation of waste gases by the greatly increased human population
Enteric fermentation in the growing numbers of ruminant farm livestock
Complete combustion of coal and petroleum in vehicles and power stations
Escape of ancient methane trapped in bubbles in melting polar ice
optionWhy: A student who thinks population growth raises greenhouse gases through breathing picks this. Exhaled gases return carbon recently fixed by photosynthesis and are not a source of methane.

Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly. Rice paddies, landfill and leakage from fossil fuel extraction are other anthropogenic sources.
A student who assumes every greenhouse gas is a combustion product picks this. Complete combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide; methane is itself a fuel that combustion consumes.

A student who pictures greenhouse gas as ancient bubbles trapped in ice picks this. Ice sheets are not a store of methane, and the anthropogenic rise comes from enteric fermentation in livestock, rice paddies, landfill and leakage of natural gas during fossil fuel extraction and transport.
questions.explain: Methanogenic archaea in the guts of cattle and other ruminants release methane, and livestock numbers have risen greatly. Rice paddies, landfill and leakage from fossil fuel extraction are other anthropogenic sources.

questions.q: In a survey of forests in the eastern United States, seedlings of several northern tree species were found on average further north than mature trees of the same species, while at the southern edge of the range there were mature trees but few seedlings. What does this indicate?
options: The ranges are shifting northward, with seedlings establishing beyond the northern edge and the range contracting at the southern edge.
The mature trees are themselves migrating northward as individuals, leaving the southern part of their range behind them.
The species are expanding their ranges, since seedlings are appearing in the north while mature trees remain in the south.
The species are unaffected by warming, because trees of some age are still present right across the whole of the range.
optionWhy: Trees shift range across generations. Seeds that establish north of the current adults extend the range northward, and failure of seedlings in the south means the southern edge will retreat as the mature trees die: northward spread with range contraction.
A student who pictures a range shift as individuals moving picks this. Rooted trees cannot move; the shift happens through seed dispersal and the survival of seedlings over generations.
A student who reads any shift as expansion picks this. Few seedlings in the south means that edge will not be replaced when the adults die, so the range contracts there.
A student who thinks species simply move with the climate unharmed picks this. The lack of regeneration in the south shows the range is being lost there.
questions.explain: Trees shift range across generations. Seeds that establish north of the current adults extend the range northward, and failure of seedlings in the south means the southern edge will retreat as the mature trees die: northward spread with range contraction.
